description:
Location: `crate-jmap-chat-client/src/methods/mod.rs:1187-1208`

  #[non_exhaustive]
  #[derive(Debug, Default)]
  pub struct PushSubscriptionPatch<'a> {
      /// Replace the verification code (set after receiving a PushVerification
      /// payload). `None` = no change.
      pub verification_code: Option<&'a str>,   // <-- ownership-proof secret
      ...
  }

CONCERN
`verification_code` is the RFC 8620 §7.2 push-subscription-ownership-proof secret. The server delivers it out-of-band (via the configured push URL); the client then echoes it back in a `PushSubscription/set` update to prove receipt. An attacker who learns the code can hijack the push subscription — they can claim ownership of subscriptions registered by other clients to the same account.

The struct derives `Debug` directly. Any `{:?}`-format of a PushSubscriptionPatch (the canonical builder type for the `update` map argument of `PushSubscription/set`) leaks the verification code:
- Application-layer logging at the SDK boundary on the verification round-trip
- Test fixtures showing how to use the API
- Future tracing instrumentation on the client surface
- The doc-comment at line 1190 invites callers to construct this struct with the secret in hand — exactly the moment a debugging println would be most tempting

Same class as JMAP-sc1b.79 (BearerAuth/BasicAuth) applied to a different secret-bearing type.

WHAT GOES WRONG
Confidentiality / hijacking — the push-subscription ownership proof is leaked, allowing an attacker who reads the log to register as the owner of a push subscription that the legitimate client created.

PROPOSED FIX
1. Remove `Debug` from the derive list at line 1188.
2. Add a manual Debug impl that redacts `verification_code` to `Some("[REDACTED]")` / `None` while showing the other fields verbatim.
3. Add a regression test that constructs PushSubscriptionPatch with a canary verification_code and asserts the canary does not appear in `{:?}` output.

ORACLE
- Canonical: JMAP-sc1b.79 fix for BearerAuth/BasicAuth in auth.rs:183-189 + test at auth.rs:443-475.
- RFC 8620 §7.2 defines the push-subscription verification code as a secret known only to the server and the client receiving the push.

RISK CLASSIFICATION
P2. Live confidentiality defect on the canonical client-side API for push-subscription verification.
